reference: AraLearn didactic model and non-punitive study state at commit 9bff37e
scope: microsequence, prerequisites, authored review, worked examples, fading, learner choice, interruption and offline resumption
key_finding: AraLearn uses author-ordered microsequences with explicit dependencies; structural completion is not mastery; review is authored or learner-marked; examples and support are placed manually; a local cursor supports resumption without attempt or time telemetry.
critical_limit: One situated personal profile; no automated scheduler, mastery gate, calibrated equivalent-item bank, or formal institutional course policy.
p2_implication: Preserve as reference values while separating structural progress, mastery, sequencing, review, support and resumption into independent dimensions.
access_status: primary documentation and source-grounded audit verified

reference: ARA Package P1 / PR #45
scope: practice, response, attempts, reveal, feedback, consequences and accessibility precedence
key_finding: P1 accepted composable practice dimensions and deferred mastery, progression, equivalent-item evidence and review sequencing to P2.
critical_limit: Does not define progression, scheduling or support policies.
p2_implication: P2 must use practice purpose, retry target, hint access, consequence level and accessibility precedence without altering P1.

reference: Kulik, Kulik & Bangert-Drowns (1990), Effectiveness of Mastery Learning Programs, DOI 10.3102/00346543060002265
scope: 108 controlled evaluations across upper elementary, secondary and college education
key_finding: Mastery-learning programs improved examination performance and attitudes, often benefiting weaker learners, but increased instructional time and self-paced college implementations sometimes reduced completion.
critical_limit: Older and heterogeneous interventions; mastery procedures, designs and content varied substantially.
p2_implication: Mastery is a defensible optional progression policy, but threshold, remediation, pace, completion risk and override must be explicit.
access_status: publisher abstract and institutional metadata verified

reference: Cook et al. (2013), Mastery Learning for Health Professionals Using Technology-Enhanced Simulation, DOI 10.1097/ACM.0b013e31829a365d
scope: 82 simulation-based mastery studies in health professions
key_finding: Mastery simulation was associated with large skill effects versus no intervention and moderate patient-outcome effects; implementations combined standards, repetition, feedback and variable learning time.
critical_limit: High-cost simulation and health-profession context; package components cannot be isolated cleanly.
p2_implication: Progression claims must record domain, criterion, feedback, repetition and evidence type rather than a generic mastery flag.

reference: Pérez & Verdín (2023), A Systematic Literature Review for Mastery Learning in Undergraduate Engineering Courses
scope: 23 undergraduate engineering mastery-learning articles
key_finding: Implementations varied widely, often centered on reassessment; students generally preferred mastery approaches, while learning and instructor-burden evidence remained inconsistent.
critical_limit: Small heterogeneous corpus, varied instruments and limited causal evidence.
p2_implication: Formal-course mastery profiles need workload, reassessment, deadline and completion policies; no universal threshold or grading model.

reference: Matayoshi et al. (2025), Using a Randomized Experiment to Compare Mastery Learning Thresholds, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15698758
scope: two mastery thresholds in ALEKS with retention and struggle moderators
key_finding: A higher threshold reduced forgetting initially, but the difference diminished over time and varied by struggle and subject; higher thresholds also create overpractice risk.
critical_limit: Vendor-specific scoring rules, mathematical topics and proprietary adaptive context.
p2_implication: Threshold is a versioned parameter tied to estimator, evidence and horizon; ARA must not encode a universal number-correct rule.

reference: Karich, Burns & Maki (2014), Updated Meta-Analysis of Learner Control Within Educational Technology, DOI 10.3102/0034654314526064
scope: 18 studies, 29 effects and 3,618 learners
key_finding: Overall learner control had near-zero average academic effects; pace, sequence, practice and review control were not uniformly beneficial.
critical_limit: Older technology, small corpus and heterogeneous definitions of control.
p2_implication: Separate pace, order, practice and review authority; learner control should be supported and bounded rather than an all-or-nothing product principle.

reference: Tabbers & de Koeijer (2010), Learner Control in Animated Multimedia Instructions, DOI 10.1007/s11251-009-9119-4
scope: learner-paced versus system-paced multimedia instruction
key_finding: Learner pacing improved transfer but substantially increased time on task, with large individual differences in control use.
critical_limit: Single multimedia context and time-efficiency trade-off.
p2_implication: Pacing authority and time budget must be distinct; learner pace can be default without implying unrestricted sequence control.
access_status: open full text and ERIC record verified

reference: Rey et al. (2019), A Meta-Analysis of the Segmenting Effect, DOI 10.1007/s10648-018-9456-4
scope: 56 investigations and 88 pairwise comparisons
key_finding: Meaningful segmentation produced small-to-medium retention and transfer benefits and lower cognitive load, while increasing learning time.
critical_limit: Mostly multimedia instructions; segment quality and prior knowledge varied.
p2_implication: Segment boundaries, coherence and control require parameters; micro-units must preserve continuity rather than become arbitrary fragments.

reference: Mawson & Kang (2025), The Distributed Practice Effect on Classroom Learning, DOI 10.3390/bs15060771
scope: 22 reports, 31 effects and more than 3,000 learners in authentic classrooms
key_finding: Distributed practice moderately outperformed massed practice; effects varied by retention interval, education level, re-exposures and implementation.
critical_limit: Only 22 applied reports and limited moderator power.
p2_implication: Review schedule is accepted, but interval pattern, target horizon, number of exposures and domain remain explicit; no universal schedule.
access_status: open full text and PubMed verified

reference: Martinengo et al. (2024), Spaced Digital Education for Health Professionals, DOI 10.2196/57760
scope: 23 randomized or quasi-randomized studies of online and simulation-based spacing
key_finding: Spaced digital education improved knowledge, some clinical behavior and surgical skills compared with massed or inactive controls.
critical_limit: Most studies had unclear/high risk of bias; domain concentration and intervention heterogeneity.
p2_implication: Digital spacing is viable across knowledge and skill profiles, but modality, interval and outcome must be recorded separately.
access_status: open full text and PubMed verified

reference: Kim & Webb (2022), The Effects of Spaced Practice on Second Language Learning, DOI 10.1111/lang.12479
scope: 48 experiments, 98 effects and 3,411 learners
key_finding: Spacing had medium-to-large effects; longer gaps helped delayed tests more, while equal and expanding schedules were statistically equivalent.
critical_limit: Second-language learning and varied targets/practice types.
p2_implication: Equal versus expanding cannot be a universal default; target retention horizon and activity type must control schedule interpretation.

reference: Carpenter, Pan & Butler (2022), The Science of Effective Learning with Spacing and Retrieval Practice, DOI 10.1038/s44159-022-00089-1
scope: mechanisms, educational applications and metacognition across spacing and retrieval
key_finding: Spacing and retrieval support lasting learning, but optimal implementation depends on retention goals, successful retrieval, feedback and learner judgments.
critical_limit: Narrative synthesis rather than one pooled intervention estimate.
p2_implication: ARA should describe objective, interval, retrieval success and review burden rather than promise an optimal algorithm.

reference: Chen, Paas & Sweller (2021), Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases, DOI 10.1007/s10648-021-09613-w
scope: 119 experimental studies after multi-database screening
key_finding: Spacing and interleaving are distinct: spacing separates study episodes, whereas interleaving supports discrimination among confusable categories.
critical_limit: The proposed mechanisms are theoretical interpretations and study designs often confound the strategies.
p2_implication: Use separate parameters for temporal distribution and category/order mixing.

reference: Brunmair & Richter (2019), Similarity Matters, DOI 10.1037/bul0000209
scope: 59 studies, 238 effects and 158 samples
key_finding: Interleaving showed a moderate overall benefit, strongest for discriminating similar categories; effects varied by material and blocking sometimes won for words.
critical_limit: Laboratory-heavy corpus and substantial domain moderation.
p2_implication: Interleaving is an author/research policy for discriminative goals, not a universal sequence default.
access_status: PubMed abstract and supplemental data verified

reference: Firth, Rivers & Boyle (2021), A Systematic Review of Interleaving as a Concept Learning Strategy, DOI 10.1002/rev3.3266
scope: 26 studies; 17 studies and 32 datasets in meta-analysis
key_finding: Interleaving benefited memory and transfer especially when category differences were subtle, including delayed tests.
critical_limit: Dominated by laboratory studies with university participants.
p2_implication: ARA must record discrimination objective, category similarity, delay and classroom authenticity.
access_status: open publisher full text and ERIC verified

reference: Rowlandson & Simpson (2025), Interleaving in Mathematical Category Learning, ERIC EJ1472022
scope: Grade 7 learning of angle-relation categories
key_finding: Two large classroom experiments repeatedly failed to detect an interleaving advantage over blocking for defined mathematical categories.
critical_limit: One topic and age group; does not refute all interleaving.
p2_implication: Domain evidence can override generic recommendations; interleaving remains optional and hypothesis-linked.

reference: Sweller & Cooper (1985), The Use of Worked Examples as a Substitute for Problem Solving in Learning Algebra, DOI 10.1207/s1532690xci0201_3
scope: initial algebra skill acquisition
key_finding: Worked examples reduced inefficient novice search and improved early learning compared with conventional problem solving.
critical_limit: Structured algebra and novice learners.
p2_implication: Examples are recommended for initial structured skills but require expertise, domain and transfer qualification.

reference: Schwonke et al. (2009), The Worked-Example Effect: Not an Artefact of Lousy Control Conditions, DOI 10.1016/j.chb.2008.12.011
scope: faded examples added to a cognitive tutor
key_finding: Faded examples improved learning efficiency and conceptual understanding even against supported problem solving.
critical_limit: Specific tutor and mathematical/procedural setting.
p2_implication: Example availability and fading are legitimate dimensions but not universal requirements.

reference: Zeitlhofer & Zumbach (2026), Sequencing Problem Solving and Worked Examples, DOI 10.1016/j.ijer.2026.103039
scope: 124 participants learning mathematical equations in four instructional sequences
key_finding: Sequences containing problem solving outperformed worked-examples-only; mixed sequences did not yield a single dominant order.
critical_limit: Single domain and short intervention.
p2_implication: Worked examples must transition to active problem solving; example position should be configurable rather than fixed universally.

reference: Tetzlaff, Simonsmeier, Peters & Brod (2025), A Cornerstone of Adaptivity, DOI 10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102142
scope: expertise-reversal effects across instructional assistance contexts
key_finding: Assistance benefits novices more reliably than it harms experts; effects vary by educational status and domain.
critical_limit: Adaptation requires valid expertise measures; evidence is less clear in some humanities/language contexts.
p2_implication: Support and fading depend on declared or assessed prerequisite state; assistance for novices has priority over aggressive removal for experts.
access_status: open article metadata and abstract verified

reference: Belland et al. (2017), Synthesizing Computer-Based Scaffolding in STEM Education, DOI 10.3102/0034654316670999
scope: 144 studies and 333 outcomes in problem-centered STEM learning
key_finding: Computer-based scaffolding had a positive average cognitive effect; benefits persisted across learner groups and assessment levels, while fading logic did not produce a clear universal moderator.
critical_limit: Heterogeneous supports and considerable between-study variation.
p2_implication: Scaffold type and availability are accepted; automatic fading is not assumed superior.

reference: Kim, Belland & Walker (2018), Effectiveness of Computer-Based Scaffolding in PBL for STEM, DOI 10.1007/s10648-017-9419-1
scope: computer scaffolds in STEM problem-based learning
key_finding: Scaffolding produced a small-to-moderate positive cognitive effect after accounting for small-study uncertainty.
critical_limit: Problem-based STEM focus and broad scaffold categories.
p2_implication: Scaffolding can support complex work, but type, purpose, authority and persistence must be explicit.
access_status: open full text and ERIC verified

reference: Renkl, Atkinson & Große (2004), How Fading Worked Solution Steps Works, DOI 10.1023/B:TRUC.0000021815.74806.F6
scope: stepwise transition from examples to independent problem solving
key_finding: Completion problems and fading can bridge example study and independent solution when support removal follows task structure.
critical_limit: Structured tasks and designed fading sequences.
p2_implication: Fading direction, trigger and granularity are parameters; removing essential problem information is prohibited.
access_status: project bibliography and journal metadata verified

reference: Monk, Trafton & Boehm-Davis (2008), The Effect of Interruption Duration and Demand on Resuming Suspended Goals, DOI 10.1037/a0014402
scope: resumption after interruptions in hierarchical interactive tasks
key_finding: Longer and more demanding interruptions increased resumption time; goal rehearsal and context affected recovery.
critical_limit: General task-performance research, not educational outcomes.
p2_implication: ARA needs explicit resume state and context cues, especially for fragmented mobile study.

reference: Foroughi et al. (2016), Individual Differences in Working-Memory Capacity and Task Resumption, DOI 10.1037/xlm0000251
scope: 229 participants, three interruption durations and working-memory measurement
key_finding: Longer interruptions increased resumption lag, especially for participants with lower working-memory capacity.
critical_limit: Procedural task and non-instructional outcome.
p2_implication: Resume support is an accessibility and cognitive-load safeguard, not merely convenience.

reference: Srivastava et al. (2021), Mitigating Reading Interruptions by Providing Reviews and Previews, arXiv 2104.06603
scope: mobile reading with post-interruption reviews or previews
key_finding: Participants preferred reviews, while previews after interruption showed larger comprehension benefits in the pilots.
critical_limit: Preprint, pilot samples and reading-specific tasks.
p2_implication: Resumption support may offer prior-summary and next-step cues, but default wording needs later UX validation.

reference: Cepeda et al. (2008), Spacing Effects in Learning: A Temporal Ridgeline, DOI 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02209.x
scope: study-gap and retention-interval combinations
key_finding: The effective spacing interval changed with the desired retention interval rather than following one fixed schedule.
critical_limit: Controlled verbal learning and limited translation to complex curricula.
p2_implication: Review target horizon is required; the product must not claim one ideal interval.
access_status: project bibliography and publisher metadata verified
